entry.dc:title: Influence of stratification of reclaimed slopes of dumps on water regime
entry.dc:creator: Kuráž V.
entry.dc:description: Reclamation of surface dumps, where the waste earth from surface mining is collected, seems to be very important technical problem. At the present time, the following variants of reclamation of the dump surface are used: surface covered by 10 to 20 cm of different organic matter and mixture of organic matter and the basic earth of the dump. The influence of stratification of soil profile in the case, when hydraulic functions of layers are significantly different have been tested in laboratory conditions. The results were compared with those of numerical simulation using model BOWAM and with results of field measurements. It was proved, that the covering of the surface of the dump using organic matter negatively influences water regime. Total amount of rainfall is consumed by the organic matter and due to stratification of soil profile and significantly lower hydraulic conductivity of basic material water is not able to penetrate to deeper parts of the profile.

entry.dc:title: The development of highwall mining systems
entry.dc:creator: Seear P.
entry.dc:description: Highwall mining has existed in many forms for several decades. This paper analyses the recent advance in highwall mining with the development of the Addcar mining system. The paper provides an historical perspective of various systems over the last 30 years.

entry.dc:title: Hard rock overburden - a basalt 'quarry' in a clay pit
entry.dc:creator: Ladnorg U.
entry.dc:description: When winning raw ceramic materials in a surface mining operation, overburden layers to be cleared are currently up to 30 m thick. To some extent, these overlying layers are composed of hard rock in the form of basalt. The movement of a such overburden represents a distinctive problem, since typical overburden technology is oriented to the clearing of loose rock such as, gravel, sand, clay and tuff, which account to a great extent for the predominant share of the overlying layers. Clearing of compact basalt requires the utilisation of methods taken from hard rock quarrying operations.

entry.dc:title: Development of welded structures for mining equipment
entry.dc:creator: Powers B.
entry.prism:publicationName: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation
entry.dc:description: The trend in equipment selection for the surface mining industry is the use of larger but fewer machines. This puts increased demands on the reliability of these machines since a single breakdown can significantly reduce a mines output. To meet these higher availability requirements, the Harnischfeger Corporation utilizes contemporary design methods coupled with innovative manufacturing processes to develop the large, welded structures which are used in today's surface mining equipment.

entry.dc:title: An evaluation of habitat rehabilitation on coastal dune forests in Northern KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa
entry.dc:creator: Van Aarde R.J.
entry.dc:description: The rehabilitation program conducted by Richards Bay Minerals (RBM) of areas exposed to opencast surface mining of sand dunes north of Richards Bay (28°43′S, 32°12′E) on the coast of northern KwaZulu-Natal Province commenced 16 years before this study and has resulted in the development of a series of known-aged stands of vegetation. By assuming that these spatially separated stands develop along a similar pathway over time, instantaneous sampling should reveal successional or other changes usually associated with aging and should provide an opportunity to evaluate the success of rehabilitation. We compare relative densities of pioneer and secondary species, species richness, and a similarity index of the herbaceous layer, tree, beetle, millipede, bird, and small-mammal communities of rehabilitating areas of known age with those of 30-year-old unmined forests and unmined forests of unknown age adjacent to the rehabilitating area. Species richness for all but the mammalian taxa increased with increasing age of rehabilitating stands. For all taxa but the mammals and herbaceous layer, the unmined stands harbored more species than the mined rehabilitating stands. The relative densities of pioneer species of all the taxa decreased with an increase in the age of rehabilitating stands, whereas those of the secondary species increased with an increase in habitat age. Similarity between unmined stands and rehabilitating stands of different ages increased with increasing regeneration age of rehabilitating stands, suggesting that rehabilitating communities, in terms of species composition and relative densities, are developing towards the status of unmined communities. Rehabilitation based on RBM's management program of limited interference is occurring and may result in the reestablishment of a coastal dune forest ecosystem. But rehabilitation resulting from succession depends on the availability of species sources from which colonization can take place. In the Richards Bay mining operation the present mining path is laid out so that such refuges are present.

entry.dc:title: Preserving natural environments on coal lands at minimum cost
entry.dc:creator: Watson W.
entry.dc:description: In the U.S., about 67 billion tons of coal (27% of the nation's surface minable coal) have been placed off-limits to surface mining by the Federal Land Policy Management Act and other restrictions in order to protect the environment. By the year 2005, it is projected that this reduction in coal reserves will add about $500 million per year to the nation's energy costs. As set-aside costs grow and the locked-up coal is perceived as progressively more valuable over time, it is likely that pressure will be brought on the U.S. Department of the Interior to revise its resource management plans. As a general rule, a rational management objective is to achieve a given amount of environmental preservation at the lowest cost. This paper provides an analytic framework, namely constrained cost minimization, for implementing that objective. Examples are given for protecting sage grouse and eagle habitat.

entry.dc:title: Potential applications of EDP in surface mining
entry.dc:creator: Stoll R.
entry.dc:description: The Department of Mining Engineering III of the Technical University, Aachen, increasingly combines commercially available and self-developed software systems in the planning of complex quarry operations. The use of such computer programs permits the simulation of deposits, systems of working, also the deployment of different equipment types for loading, transporting and crushing. Within short times the active operations of a quarry or the use of specific equipment can be simulated, including cost calculations. Alternatives can be developed and compared in order to select the best solution or to optimize operations. This paper presents the potential of such computer programs by the way of extracts from a recent planning project for a quarry in Germany.

entry.dc:title: Development in exploration, evaluation and exploitation of cement raw materials
entry.dc:creator: Kumar V.
entry.prism:publicationName: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
entry.dc:description: Computers are playing an increasingly important role in geological exploration, evaluation and mine planning. Their capability to significantly increase the interpretative skills, efficiency and productivity of both explorationists and mine planners has bean proved beyond doubt. This paper focuses on the computer capabilities and its application in formulating exploration strategies and assessing mineral deposits, etc. apart from highlighting the salient features of available commercial softwares. An overview of technological advancements in surface mining methods and haulage systems, particularly from environmental angle is also presented.

entry.dc:title: Sulfide oxidation in brown coal overburden and chemical modeling of reactions in aquifers influenced by sulfide oxidation
entry.dc:creator: van Berk W.
entry.dc:description: Surface mining of brown coal in the Rhineland brown coal mining area (Germany) causes acidification of pyritic sandy overburden sediments. Convective transport of air, indicated by an enrichment of nitrogen gas in oxidized overburden, is, in addition to diffusion of oxygen, the driving mechanism for sulfide oxidation. Products of sulfide oxidation (2SO<inf>4</inf><sup>2-</sup> + 2H<sup>+</sup> + Fe<sup>2+</sup>) stored in acidic material in the overburden dump are leached by groundwater filling the dump and react with the carbonate phases of nonacidic material. The resulting hydrochemical composition (up to 6000 mg l<sup>-1</sup> SO<inf>4</inf><sup>2-</sup>, 3000 mg l<sup>-1</sup> Fe<sup>2+</sup>, pH 4.5) in groundwaters is controlled by simultaneous solubility equilibria with CaSO<inf>4</inf>·2H<inf>2</inf>O<inf>(s)</inf>, Fe(OH)<inf>3(s)</inf>, Fe<inf>0.9</inf>Ca<inf>0.1</inf>CO<inf>3(s)</inf> and CO<inf>2(g)</inf>. Calculated equilibrium concentrations of major components and pH in groundwater, partial pressure of CO<inf>2(g)</inf> in soil gas, and coupled mass transfer match observed conditions. © 1995 Springer-Verlag.

entry.dc:title: Servicing Olympic Dam
entry.dc:creator: Chadwick J.
entry.dc:description: Product support/service agreements are becoming more common around in the mining industry. Led by surface mining, the underground sector is also now beginning to develop such relationship between supplier and mining company. A good example of this agreement is between Tamrock and Olympic Dam. Both parties benefit greatly from the agreement. Olympic Dam report that it saves money in equipment maintenance and parts and benefited from increased machine availability and reliability. Tamrock safeguards its parts sales from 'pirates' and generates more business with the Olympic Dam, while both parties able to benefit from product development in a very high productivity underground operation.

entry.dc:title: Optimizing mine life and design capacity
entry.dc:creator: Hajdasinski M.
entry.prism:publicationName: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
entry.dc:description: In his recent paper, “A theoretical approach to determination of mine life and design capacity,” (International Journal of Surface Mining, vol.3, 1989, pp. 49-50), Z. Li maintains that, under the reinvestment assumption, the objective functions of models for the optimization of mine life and design capacity should be based on the Net Future Value rather than on the Net Present Value concept. The current contribution proves that, in fact, the opposite is true, and that the Net Future Value would make models with unconstrained time variable, like Li's model, undefined. It is also demonstrated that Li's sensitivity analysis is misleading, as are his optimization results, since meaningful optimal solutions cannot be obtained from his optimization model. © 1995, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC. entry.dc:title: Lung cancer in former bismuth workers (1992)
entry.dc:creator: Bruske-Hohlfeld I.
entry.dc:description: As part of a case-control study on lung cancer risk and exposure to indoor radon, 93 patients with lung cancer were detected who had been employed in a uranium mining company in the former German Democratic Republic. The youngest patient was 51 and the oldest 78 years old. Employment was started in nearly every case before 1955. 81 of the 93 patients had had occupational exposure to radon and its progeny. 78 worked as miners or craftsmen underground and 3 were employed in surface mining or uranium processing. 12 men had exclusively worked above ground in jobs that involved no exposure to radon. The mean cumulative exposure was 606 WLM (Range: 2 WLM - 1791 WLM). Using the mean risk coefficient of the International Commission on Radiological Protection of 1.3%/WLM as a basis, the patients' mean lung cancer risk was increased by a factor of 9. Nearly 10% of the patients lived in the study region of West Germany. Therefore lung cancer patients should always be asked about former employment in uranium mining.

entry.dc:title: Rock anchor support systems at Smoky River Coal Limited, Grande Cache, Alberta
entry.dc:creator: Dawson R.
entry.dc:description: At Smoky River Coal Limited (SRCL), economic occurrences of structurally thickened coal deposits form attractive surface mining targets. These steeply dipping, structurally complex deposits require that special attention be given to pit wall design and operational practices. Where feasible, there is potential for reducing footwall waste requirements and/or increasing coal recovery. This paper outlines design considerations and performance of rock anchor support systems at SRCL. Three case histories are included that illustrate the design process for supporting steeply dipping footwall slopes using rock anchors. -from Authors

entry.dc:title: State-of-the-art in mountaintop removal and contour mining
entry.dc:creator: White M.
entry.dc:description: Contour mining results in low mining ratios, but also lengthy outcrop disturbances (highwalls) and numerous environmental problems. Initially, the mining ratio in a contour mine operation was less than 7 to 1. Under present regulations and coal prices, contour mining has been reduced in the US. However, it is efficient in mountaintop removal operations. Contour mining incorporated into a mountaintop removal operation helps control drainage, minimize downslope placements (overshots) and balance the mining ratios. While mountaintop removal optimizes the coal reserve, the nature of this method results in coal being produced with higher mining ratios. This is due to the topography of the mining area. However, another contributor to these ratio increases include previous mining operations in the area. The mountaintop removal method of surface mining on this reserve began during the 1970s. The top of the mountain is removed to uncover the most economically minable coal seams. The overburden and interburden removed are placed in valley fills and backstacked on previously mined areas as required to produce the coal. Under ideal conditions, it is possible to extract nearly 100% of the minable coal, except for the outcrop barriers. -from Authors

entry.dc:title: Wildlife Management, Surface Mining, and Regional Planning
entry.dc:creator: NIEMAN T.
entry.dc:description: ABSTRACT Wildlife management, surface mining, and regional planning historically have had conflicting missions. The cooperative public/private venture which created the Robinson Forest and Cyprus‐Amax Wildlife Management Areas is presented as an example of how a regional perspective encourages a symbiotic relationship among these Functions. Wildlife management areas, as either an interim or final land use. are shown to incorporate development concepts which benefit the general public, the coal industry, and the environment. Examining the regional pattern or wildlife management areas and refuges confirms the appropriateness of the subject site for this use. It is suggested that the pattern of mined lands can be studied to identify other sites with potential to provide linkages between wildlife habitat areas and encourage reclamation of such sites to the “fish and wildlife” postmining land use. Such reclamation strategies should be pursued within a long‐term planning framework. More research is needed to recreate specific habitat types on drastically disturbed land and planning is needed to assure that sensitive habitats or species arc located away from zones likely to undergo future development. Use of geographic information systems to integrate existing environmental information could make such studies more effective. Copyright © 1995, Wiley Blackwell. All rights reserved

entry.dc:title: Characterizing rare plant habitat for restoration in the San Bernardino National Forest
entry.dc:creator: Gonella M.P.
entry.prism:publicationName: General Technical Report US Department of Agriculture Forest Service
entry.dc:description: Surface mining of limestone in the San Bernardino Mountains has caused loss of native vegetation and of habitat for four carbonate-endemic plant taxa. This paper characterizes features of carbonate substrates and of habitat occupied by two of these species: cushenbury milkvetch (Astragalus albens) and Cushenbury buckwheat (Eriogonum ovalifolium var. Vineum) to assist in developing revegetation success criteria for mined lands. Carbonate substrates in the San Bernardino Mountains were vegetationally and floristically distinct from non-carbonate substrates. Habitats occupied by Cushenbury milkvetch and Cushenbury buckwheat were distinguished from general carbonate substrate by higher % soil calcium, different slope angles, surface soil characteristics, and floristic composition. -from Authors

entry.dc:title: Environmental issues of the Appalachian coal region
entry.dc:creator: Kleinmann R.L.P.
entry.dc:description: Mining has been a significant component of the Appalachian economy for about 200 yr. The region continues to be adversely affected by the environmental degradation associated with these past activities. In addition, companies today are being denied permits at sites where acid generation appears likely. And air emission limitations at power plants now threaten the economic health of many moderate- to high-sulfur coal mines. Thus, when considering the environmental impacts of mining coal in Appalachia, it is important to consider abandoned and active mine issues. For example, abandoned mines generate acidic, iron-rich waters that adversely affect more than 6400 km (4000 miles) of rivers and streams in Appalachia. In contrast, operations that were active after the enactment of the 1977 Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act (SMCRA) cause little water pollution. Subsidence in the region results from the degradation of abandoned, shallow room-and-pillar mines and from high-extraction deep mining. Several field studies revealed that the maximum vertical displacement can be as much as 60% of the extracted thickness. About 1.5 m (5 ft) of coal extracted can produce as much as 0.9 m (3 ft) of vertical movement. This maximum movement occurs over the center of the extracted area and vertical movement decreases laterally outwards. Above the edges of the extracted area, subsidence is generally less than 13 mm (6 in.) and decreases to zero within several hundred feet. Air quality is perhaps the only environmental issue that is associated almost exclusively with active operations. -from Authors

entry.dc:title: Depicting California's critical environmental zones
entry.dc:creator: Pryde P.
entry.prism:publicationName: Yearbook Association of Pacific Coast Geographers
entry.dc:description: A set of critical environmental area maps for the state of California has been prepared. These maps show regions of the state where the natural environment has been adversely affected by the consequences of economic activities, in some cases exacerbated by natural conditions. Environmental topics mapped include air pollution, pollution of inland and coastal waters, hazardous wastes, surface mining, and deterioration of forests and sensitive habitats. Initially, for clarity, mapping was done on three separate sheets, under the topic headings of water problems, habitat problems, and air and toxic pollutants. Subsequently, all of the data were combined onto a single comprehensive map. This resultant map illustrates by means of overlapping areal and point symbols the generalized locales and regions of concentrations of contemporary environmental problems in California.

entry.dc:title: An evaluation of fluidized bed combustor ash as a source of alkalinity to treat toxic rock materials
entry.dc:creator: Renton J.
entry.dc:description: The coal mining industry is in need of effective, locally available, low-cost ameliorants that can be used to treat the toxic materials generated by surface mining and coal cleaning plants. Ashes generated by fluidized bed combustors may locally fit these criteria. Samples of fly ash and bottom ash were acquired from facilities in West Virginia, Texas, and California and evaluated for their ability to generate alkalinity. The results show that FBC ash has the potential to produce solutions of high alkalinity depending on the CaO and CaCO<inf>3</inf> contents. The relative content of CaO, and to a lesser extent Ca(OH)<inf>2</inf>, determines the rate at which alkalinity will be produced. The neutralization potential is the best parameter to evaluate the potential of an FBC ash to produce alkalinity. Because the composition of ashes from a facility vary over time and because no single parameter will accurately evaluate the rate at which alkalinity will be produced, the rate of alkaline production must be evaluated by controlled leach experiments. © 1996.

entry.dc:title: Nitrogen loss from a soil restored after surface mining
entry.dc:creator: Davies R.
entry.dc:description: Anaerobic conditions develop below about 1-m depth in soil stock-piles and this can lead to an accumulation of ammonium (NH<inf>4</inf><sup>+</sup>) and transformations of a normally relatively inert organic-N pool within the soil. After reinstatement of the soil from the stockpile, the NH<inf>4</inf><sup>+</sup> may rapidly be transformed to nitrate (NO<inf>3</inf><sup>-</sup>) and lost from the soil with the labile organic-N. These losses may lead to a pollution risk in addition to the loss of a resource. The magnitude of N losses were measured from a soil that had been reinstated for agricultural use after being stored in a stockpile for 12 yr. Nitrogen movement in the soil profile and losses into the water-course were monitored for 2 yr beginning immediately after reinstatement. Relatively large movements of N were detected within the soil profile and large losses to the atmosphere and/or water-courses were estimated. Over the 2-yr monitoring period, 2449 kg ha<sup>-1</sup> of N was lost from the soil profile; 90% of this was not accounted for either in the soil or in the runoff or drainage water as mineral-N and was presumed to have entered either the atmosphere or aquatic environment as organic-N. To aid remedial measures, the proportion entering the atmosphere as nitrogen and nitrous oxides or the aquatic environment as organic-N, needs further investigation.

entry.dc:title: Geogenically Acidified Mining Lakes — Living Conditions and Possibilities of Restoration
entry.dc:creator: Klapper H.
entry.prism:publicationName: Internationale Revue Der Gesamten Hydrobiologie Und Hydrographie
entry.dc:description: Pyrite and marcasite oxidation in the consequence of lignite surface mining creates lakes with pH as low as 2 to 3, buffered by high contents of iron and aluminium. Living conditions in this extreme habitat for plants and animals are described as well as the characteristics of the pioneer settlement. The utilization of these fish‐free lakes is very limited. As possibilities for a water quality improvement special recultivation methods of overburden, chemical neutralization and biological ecotechnologies are recommended.
